author: Tanjamul Azad

provenance.case: HMRC and Behavioural Insights Team social-norm tax letters (2011-2012 trials)

references.citation: Hallsworth, M., List, J. A., Metcalfe, R. D., Vlaev, I. (2017). The behavioralist as tax collector: Using natural field experiments to enhance tax compliance. Journal of Public Economics 148, 14-31.
NBER Working Paper 20007 (2014), same authors and title.

target.task: Our university library in Chattogram lends about 3,000 books a month. 86% of loans are returned on time; the rest are late, and late books are the main reason students cannot get course texts before exams. Plan the reminder messages for borrowers whose books are overdue.

rules.text: Give each message a day number counted from the due date, in increasing order, none later than day 30.
Each message text has at most 60 words.
Use only facts given in this brief; do not invent statistics.
The late fine stays at 5 BDT per day.

target.format: Reply with JSON only, in this shape: {"messages": [{"day": 1, "channel": "email or sms", "text": "..."}], "fine_per_day_bdt": 5}

source_example.text: In 2011 and 2012 the UK tax authority, HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC), worked with the Behavioural Insights Team on letters to people who had not paid tax due under Self Assessment. The standard reminder letter stated the debt and the penalty for late payment. Trial versions added one sentence about what other people do, for example: "Nine out of ten people in the UK pay their tax on time." One version went further and said: "You are currently in the very small minority of people who have not paid us yet." The first trial covered roughly a hundred thousand people with Self Assessment debts. The researchers measured how many people paid within 23 days of the letter. Messages that described the social norm raised that share compared with the standard letter. In the first trial, the minority sentence produced the largest effect of the messages tested. Because only the wording changed, the extra tax was brought in at almost no cost, and the authors estimated it in millions of pounds. The study was published by Hallsworth, List, Metcalfe and Vlaev in the Journal of Public Economics in 2017. Its lesson is that people respond to what they believe others like them do. The same researchers stress that a norm message only helps when the norm is true and favourable.

incidental_details.text: The UK statistic 'nine out of ten'
